\subsection{Photoionization}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{sections/figure_keldysh}}
    \caption{Illustration of the different regimes of ionization.}
    \label{fig:regimes_ionisation}
\end{figure}

Strong focusing leads to high optical intensity within the material. This high concentration of photons in the same spot increases the probability of multiphoton ionization, a nonlinear effect \cite{mao2004}. The more intense the field, the more the potential binding the electron to the ion is distorted. Beyond a certain intensity threshold, the barrier takes on a triangular shape and becomes thin enough to allow for tunneling ionization. The Keldysh parameter was introduced to distinguish between the regime of dominant multiphoton ionization and the regime of dominant tunneling ionization \cite{mao2004}. The Keldysh parameter corresponds to the square root of the ratio between the bandgap energy and the ponderomotive energy.

In the semiclassical model, an electron escapes through a barrier of width $l = U_i/e\mathcal{E}$ with a velocity $v = \sqrt{2U_i/m}$. The time required to traverse this distance is: 
\begin{equation}
\tau_{\text{tun}} = \frac{l}{v} = \frac{U_i/e\mathcal{E}}{\sqrt{2U_i/m}} = \frac{\sqrt{2m U_i}}{e\mathcal{E}}
\end{equation}
The characteristic time during which tunneling can occur is given by $\tau \approx 1/\omega_0$.
The ratio of these times is then: 
\begin{equation}
\gamma= \frac{\tau_{\text{tun}}}{\tau} = \omega_0\frac{\sqrt{2m U_i}}{e\mathcal{E}}
\end{equation}
If the ratio $\gamma \ll 1$, it means that the tunneling traversal time is very short compared to the ionization time. Tunneling is instantaneous on the timescale of the laser cycle. The field behaves like a quasi-static field. Conversely, if $\gamma \gg 1$, the field oscillates too rapidly to allow the electron to cross the barrier via tunneling, ionization then requires multiphoton absorption \cite{bulgakova2010}.

The Keldysh photoionization rate is defined as follows:
\begin{equation}
W_{PI}(|\mathcal{E}|) = \frac{2\omega_0}{9\pi}\bigg(\frac{\omega_0m}{\hbar\sqrt{\gamma_1}}\bigg)^{\frac{3}{2}}Q(\gamma,x)\exp(-\alpha\lceil x+1\rceil)
\end{equation}
With $\gamma_1 = \frac{\gamma^2}{1+\gamma^2}$, $\gamma_2 = \frac{1}{1+\gamma^2}$ and $x = \frac{2}{\pi}\frac{U_iE(\gamma_2)}{\hbar\omega_0\sqrt{\gamma_1}}$ \begin{equation}
Q(\gamma,x) = \frac{\pi}{2K(\gamma_2)}\sum^\infty_{n=0}\exp \bigg(-n\pi\frac{K(\gamma_1)-E(\gamma_1)}{E(\gamma_2)}\bigg)\Phi\bigg(\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{n+2\lceil x + 1\rceil-2x}{K(\gamma_2)E(\gamma_2)}}\bigg)
\end{equation}

 $\Phi$ is the Dawson function $\Phi(z) = e^{-z^2}\int^z_0e^{y^2}dy$ and $K$ and $E$ are the complete elliptic integral of the first and second kind, respectively, with parameter $m = k^2 $ \begin{align}
K(m) &= \int_0^{\pi/2} [1 - m \sin(t)^2]^{-1/2} dt \\
E(m) &= \int_0^{\pi/2} [1 - m \sin(t)^2]^{1/2} dt
\end{align}

The blue dashed line corresponds to the standard perturbative MPI law ($W_{\text{MPI}} = \sigma_K I^K \rho_{\text{at}}$). The vertical gray line indicates the typical intensity clamping level ($\sim 5 \times 10^{13} \text{ W/cm}^2$) reached in 800 nm filamentation simulations.}
